questions.question: int counter() { static int c = 0; c++; return c; } int main() { int i, s=0; for(i=0;i<4;i++) s += counter(); printf("%d", s); }  What is printed?
questions.solutionApproach: Calls return 1,2,3,4 in sequence (static persists). Sum = 1+2+3+4 = 10.

questions.question: int main() { int i=5, j; j = i++ + ++i; printf("%d %d", i, j); }  What is printed? (assume left-to-right evaluation for this exercise)
questions.solutionApproach: i++ uses 5, then i becomes 6. ++i makes i=7, uses 7. j = 5+7=12. Final i=7.
questions.answer: 7 12 (note: real compilers may vary since C doesn't guarantee evaluation order here — GATE avoids truly ambiguous cases; this is a simplified drill)

questions.question: unsigned int a = 3, b = 5; printf("%u", a-b);  What gets printed (assume 32-bit unsigned int)?
A C program calls a function foo(int) before defining it, with no prototype declared. What happens?
questions.solutionApproach: In older C standards, this is allowed with implicit-int assumption (compiler assumes it returns int); modern compilers (C99+) issue a warning or error for implicit declarations depending on strictness flags. It's a common source of subtle bugs, not necessarily a hard failure.
questions.answer: Typically compiles with a warning (implicit declaration) rather than failing outright, though strict/modern compilers may error.
